..
Issued at 243 PM CDT Wed Sep 16 2026

We are starting to see sprinkles to very light showers break out 
across parts of the area this afternoon as warm air advection (WAA) 
strengthens aloft. With saturation in the low levels but a dry 
dendritic growth zone (DGZ), sprinkles/drizzle is expected. At the 
same time, low level stratus not only continues to blanket most of 
the forecast area but is lowering in height. These conditions will 
persist through the rest of the afternoon and evening hours before 
rain chances ending after midnight. Though with lowering ceilings, 
sprinkles/drizzle looks to persist through the night. At the same 
time, with sufficient low level moisture in place, ceilings look to 
lower to potentially down to fog across the area. As of now, think 
that it is mainly across the higher elevation areas along the 
Buffalo Ridge in southwest Minnesota, downs through northwest Iowa, 
and along the Missouri River Valley. With the stratus/fog in place, 
temperatures will not move much, only lowering to the 50s to low 
60s. 

Fog along with sprinkles/drizzle will continue into the morning 
hours before lifting through the morning hours. This should allow 
for temperatures to warm to the 70s for the afternoon hours. While 
the afternoon hours will be quiet, things will change Thursday 
evening and especially for Thursday night as a shortwave trough 
rounds the western flank of an upper level ridge, parked over the 
southern CONUS. This wave will strengthen low level WAA and begin to 
develop showers across central South Dakota Thursday evening. The 
WAA will be driven by the low level jet (LLJ), tightening the 
temperature gradient, resulting in frontogenesis (FGEN). This band 
of FGEN looks to be the main driver for rain as the rain becomes 
more widespread as the forcing for ascent increases. There also 
looks to be instability above the front which looks to result in a 
tighter band of rain. This tighter band of rain continues to look 
most likely near and north of highway-14. The best forcing for 
ascent will push off to the northeast of the area Friday morning, 
resulting in slowly waning rain across the area. Could still see 
lighter rain persist through the rest of the morning hours. There 
remains some uncertainty in where this heaviest band sets up. Latest 
12z deterministic guidance shows a slight wobble back southwards 
from the previous 00z guidance. However, the ensembles show similar 
placement with this band near and north of highway-14. The ensembles 
mean QPF remains a broad 0.5 inches to up to about 2.0 inches but 
their 90th percentile QPF also remains up to 2.0 to 3.0+ inches. 
Think this 90th percentile is representative of the highest amounts 
that fall within the band itself. The ensembles probabilities do 
support these totals as they all have a near 100% chance for 0.50 
inches or more of rain. The probability for an inch or more is 
between 40-90% and lowers to a 20-40% chance for 2 inches or more. 
Have slightly trended total QPF upwards and think the overall 
rainfall amounts will be a broad 0.5 inch to 2.0 inches of rain 
across the area. Locally higher amounts up to and exceeding 3.0 
inches is possible, mainly under the band itself. This may lead to 
minor rises in rivers and streams as well all ponding on roadways 
and poor drainage areas. 

A small break in the action is possible for part of the afternoon 
hours on Friday as some breaks in the clouds occur. This will allow 
for high temperatures to warm to the low 70s to mid 80s, warmest 
south of I-90. The pockets of sunshine and diurnal heating may allow 
for sufficient CAPE values to return northwards, potentially 
resulting in strong to severe storms. This potential is highly 
conditional and dependent on how quickly morning showers and cloud 
cover can exit the area. If a severe weather threat were to 
materialize, it would be Friday afternoon and evening for locations 
south of I-90.

Saturday looks to be a dry day across the area with high 
temperatures near seasonable in the upper 60s to low 70s. The break 
from the rain will be short lived as another upper level wave looks 
to eject into the Plains on Sunday. This chance for rain is 
supported by the ensembles as they show a broad 30-70% chance for 
rainfall amounts to exceed a tenth of an inch. Good news is that 
instability is not expected, so this looks to be more stratiform 
rain rather than convective rain. 

Medium range guidance diverges in how the upper level pattern will 
evolve for next week. There could be additional chances for rain but 
details are uncertain this far out. Temperatures on the other hand 
look to remain seasonable in the 60s and 70s.
